results.summary: This design transmits an asynchronous serial UART message on three separate output pins. It is intended to be tested by attaching a UART receiver to each pin and configuring the receiver for 1200 baud. External hardware needed is a serial cable or equivalent receiver for each output. The documentation is extremely thin, consisting only of a one-line description and brief testing instructions, so no further implementation details are available.

This design emulates a six-sided die by generating a pseudo-random number from 1 to 6 using a linear-feedback shift register. When the ROLL input is pulsed, the 7-segment display rapidly cycles through numbers before settling on a final value, and the decimal point lights up to indicate completion. It requires an external 7-segment display, such as the one on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, and is controlled by a clock and reset signal. The project is notable for its simple, self-contained implementation of a familiar game element on a single tile.

This design implements a timer that measures up to 99 minutes and 59 seconds by multiplexing four seven-segment displays. The documentation is essentially empty, with both the 'How it works' and 'How to test' sections marked as TODO. It requires four seven-segment displays plus 74-series logic chips to build the selection circuitry, but no further usage details are provided. Because of the missing documentation, little can be said about its internal operation or testing procedure.

This design is a purely combinational 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit numbers on its input pins and produces an 8-bit product on its output pins. It is implemented using AND gates and several adders, without any sequential logic. To use it, a user would apply the two operands via switches or other sources and read the binary result on LEDs. The project is a straightforward arithmetic building block and requires external hardware such as DIP switches and LEDs for input and output.

This design echoes a predefined text message to a 20x4 character LCD. It contains a ROM holding the text and logic to perform the initialization sequence and cursor positioning, operating from an external clock since it lacks an internal divider. The design requires a 20x4 character LCD connected according to the pinout, and optionally LEDs on two output pins. It is notable as a simple demonstration of driving a character display from a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This design implements a 6-bit Gray code counter in the Amaranth HDL. It outputs a sequence where only one bit changes between successive counts, which can help reduce switching noise in certain applications. The counter is controlled by external clock and reset signals and requires no additional hardware. The project serves as a simple educational example of Gray code and Amaranth-based design.

This design computes the square root of a 7-bit integer in 4.2 fixed-point format, rounding down to the nearest quarter. It uses Newton's method and produces a result after three clock cycles. The inputs are the 7-bit value and a clock, and the output is a 6-bit fixed-point number. Optionally, a binary-to-BCD converter can be added to display the result, but no other external hardware is required.

This design uses AND gates to drive a 7-segment display so that a '3' is shown when the first four inputs are all high. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires no external hardware beyond the display itself. The project is extremely simple and appears to be an educational exercise in combinational logic. Its documentation is minimal, but the functionality is clear from the description.

This design implements a 1-bit ALU from Tanenbaum's book, supporting AND, NOT, OR, and ADD operations selected by two mode inputs. It includes enable and invert controls for the inputs and a carry-in for addition, and the output is shown on a 7-segment display with the carry-out on the decimal point. The design is intended for educational use and can be chained to create wider ALUs. No external hardware is needed beyond the on-board display.

This design counts from 0 to 9, incrementing once per second, and displays the count on a 7-segment display. It is implemented in Wokwi using a counter and combinational logic, and is tested by setting the clock to 1 Hz and toggling reset. No external hardware is required aside from the display. The project is a simple demonstration of a slow counter and display driver.
